accepted.question_text: Determine whether every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) lies on the vertical line in the complex plane whose real part is 1/2. In other words, aside from the well-known zeros at the negative even integers, decide whether all other zeros of ζ(s) = 0 have real part exactly 1/2.

evidence.quote:
The Riemann hypothesis asserts that all interesting solutions of the equation

   ζ(s) = 0

lie on a certain vertical straight line.

accepted.question_text: Give a mathematically rigorous existence theory for quantum Yang-Mills theory and prove that it has a positive mass gap, meaning that although the underlying classical waves travel at the speed of light, the quantum particles predicted by the theory have positive masses. The task is to establish the existence of the Yang-Mills theory together with this mass-gap property from first principles.

evidence.quote: Progress in establishing the existence of the Yang-Mills theory and a mass gap will require the introduction of fundamental new ideas both in physics and in mathematics.

accepted.question_text: Decide whether every computational problem whose proposed solution can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly. Equivalently, determine whether there exist problems for which verifying a candidate answer is feasible but generating an answer by any direct procedure necessarily takes impractically long, or whether in fact every such efficiently checkable problem also has a feasible algorithm for finding solutions.

evidence.page: P vs. NP problem > Clay description
evidence.quote: one of the outstanding problems in computer science is determining whether questions exist whose answer can be quickly checked, but which require an impossibly long time to solve by any direct procedure.

accepted.question_text: Develop substantial mathematical theory for the Navier-Stokes equations that explains and predicts phenomena such as waves, breezes, and turbulence by improving our understanding of their solutions. The problem is to make decisive progress toward a rigorous theory that unlocks the behavior encoded by the Navier-Stokes equations.

evidence.quote: The challenge is to make substantial progress toward a mathematical theory which will unlock the secrets hidden in the Navier-Stokes equations.

accepted.question_text: For projective algebraic varieties, determine whether every Hodge cycle is a rational linear combination of algebraic cycles. That is, decide whether the cohomological pieces called Hodge cycles on these particularly nice spaces always come from geometric pieces called algebraic cycles after allowing rational linear combinations.

evidence.quote: The Hodge conjecture asserts that for particularly nice types of spaces called projective algebraic varieties, the pieces called Hodge cycles are actually (rational linear) combinations of geometric pieces called algebraic cycles.

accepted.question_text: Classify whether a closed three-dimensional space with the simple-connectivity property must be the three-dimensional sphere; equivalently, determine whether the 3-sphere is characterized by simple connectivity among such spaces. In this source, this problem is explicitly described as solved by Grigoriy Perelman.

evidence.quote: Poincaré, almost a hundred years ago, knew that a two dimensional sphere is essentially characterized by this property of simple connectivity, and asked the corresponding question for the three dimensional sphere.

This question turned out to be extraordinarily difficult. Nearly a century passed between its formulation in 1904 by Henri Poincaré and its solution by Grigoriy Perelman, announced in preprints posted on ArXiv.org in 2002 and 2003.

accepted.question_text: For an abelian variety, determine how the size of the group of rational points is related to the behavior of its associated zeta function near s = 1. In particular, decide whether ζ(1) = 0 exactly when there are infinitely many rational points, and whether ζ(1) ≠ 0 exactly when there are only finitely many rational points.

evidence.quote: the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture asserts that the size of the group of rational points is related to the behavior of an associated zeta function ζ(s) near the point s=1. In particular this amazing conjecture asserts that if ζ(1) is equal to 0, then there are an infinite number of rational points (solutions), and conversely, if ζ(1) is not equal to 0, then there is only a finite number of such points.
